primary_cause: Oil-price-war shock hitting Exxon earnings and cash-flow outlook. Saudi Arabia launched oil-price war. Crude plunged ~25% on Mar 9. Saudi Aramco said would raise output to 12.3M bpd from 9.7M bpd in April
secondary_factors: COVID demand destruction and broader recession fear
store_description: Exxon was one of the clearest stock-specific macro casualties. With crude down about 25% on March 9 and Saudi signaling a move to 12.3M bpd on March 10 the market was repricing a much weaker 2020 upstream profit outlook for integrated oil majors even before March 11's broader pandemic panic.

primary_cause: Broad market liquidation on pandemic fears not Walmart-specific bad news. Walmart posted Mar 10 coronavirus response update
secondary_factors: Concern that panic buying would be offset by labor cleaning stocking and supply-chain strain
store_description: Walmart actually looked relatively defensive fundamentally and by March 10 was already publicly detailing COVID operating changes. The 4.5% drop looks less like a company event and more like indiscriminate equity selling as Italy entered nationwide lockdown and the WHO declared a pandemic.

primary_cause: Rate-collapse and net-interest-margin compression fears for banks. 10-year Treasury fell below 1% for first time ever. Reuters noted S&P financials fell 3.7%
secondary_factors: Recession and credit-loss concerns from COVID escalation. Wells large spread-lending exposure made it especially vulnerable
store_description: By March 3 the 10-year Treasury yield fell below 1% for the first time ever and Reuters noted the S&P financials fell 3.7% because low rates hurt bank profitability. Wells Fargo's large spread-lending exposure made it especially vulnerable as investors moved from slower growth to possible recession plus lower-for-longer rates.

primary_cause: Expected collapse in cross-border travel payments. Travel demand deteriorating fast Italy locked down cross-border spending obvious exposure
secondary_factors: Weaker restaurant entertainment and fuel spend as social distancing accelerated. Later Visa confirmed rapid deterioration in cross-border travel-related spend
store_description: This was an early repricing of Visa's most lucrative revenue stream rather than a company press-release event. As the travel outlook worsened and border restrictions tightened investors started discounting the kind of deterioration Visa later described as a rapid drop in cross-border travel-related spending.

primary_cause: Same bank-sector rate and recession shock as WFC. Yields collapsing below historic lows. Expected credit deterioration if consumer and business activity froze
secondary_factors: Regionals and money-center banks alike repriced sharply lower. No USB-specific catalyst
store_description: U.S. Bancorp was hit by the same force crushing banks generally: yields collapsing below historic lows and investors pricing in both margin pressure and future loan losses. Once the 10-year fell below 1% and recession odds surged regionals were repriced sharply lower.

primary_cause: Fear of global shipping and B2B volume disruption from COVID. Rapidly worsening freight air-travel and cross-border disruption
secondary_factors: Concern that any e-commerce lift would be offset by lower-margin residential mix and broad industrial slowdown. No fresh UPS announcement
store_description: In early March the market was still treating parcel carriers as cyclical logistics names not yet as pandemic winners. With Italy locked down flights canceled and global trade disruption intensifying investors likely focused first on the downside to international and business shipments.

primary_cause: Industrial-volume and freight-demand fears from COVID slowdown. Railroads repriced for lower carloads
secondary_factors: Recession pricing across transport and cyclicals. No fresh Union Pacific announcement
store_description: Railroads were being repriced for lower carloads as industrial production intermodal traffic and trade expectations deteriorated. March 11 sat in the middle of the transition from virus is overseas to nationwide demand shock so UNP's decline looks mainly like a macro and transport-volume repricing.

primary_cause: No PepsiCo-specific negative. Broad-market de-risking with some concern over away-from-home consumption exposure
secondary_factors: Global supply-chain uncertainty and emerging lockdown risk. Restaurants travel venues and convenience channels under pressure
store_description: Pepsi was more defensive than most names which matches the smaller 3.3% drop. But as restaurants travel venues and convenience channels came under pressure globally the market still marked down even staples with better at-home demand characteristics.

primary_cause: Expected plunge in ride-hailing demand as people stopped traveling and commuting. Mar 7 Uber said would compensate drivers diagnosed with COVID-19 or quarantined for up to 14 days
secondary_factors: Higher driver-support costs and investor concern about gig-worker exposure. Reuters later reported demand down as much as 70% in some U.S. cities
store_description: Uber's March 7 sick-pay announcement underscored that the outbreak was already affecting its network economics. Given what later became explicit with Reuters reporting demand down as much as 70% in some U.S. cities the March 11 selloff looks like an early rational repricing of the core mobility business.

primary_cause: No fresh AT&T-specific negative. Broad market and pandemic selloff
secondary_factors: Concern about WarnerMedia advertising and entertainment exposure if outbreak worsened
store_description: AT&T was partly cushioned by the defensiveness of telecom which helps explain the 3.7% drop. Still by March 11 investors were starting to think beyond wireless service to media advertising theaters sports and general corporate-spending exposure.

primary_cause: Expected collapse in mall foot traffic and tenant sales and rent collections. Mall landlords obvious COVID casualties as lockdowns spread
secondary_factors: Rising probability of store closures and tenant distress. Simon formally shut U.S. properties Mar 18
store_description: Simon was one of the cleanest physical congregation losers in the tape. With Italy in nationwide lockdown and the WHO declaring a pandemic on March 11 the market moved quickly to price a sharp hit to occupancy economics and tenant health for enclosed malls.

primary_cause: No Southern Company-specific negative. Indiscriminate risk-off selling rather than a clear company event
secondary_factors: Utility sensitivity to funding conditions and broad equity deleveraging
store_description: Utilities were not immune during the March 2020 liquidation phase even when their fundamentals were more stable than cyclicals. Southern's 6.2% drop looks mostly like part of the forced cross-sector selloff after the Italy lockdown and pandemic declaration.

primary_cause: Fear of global store traffic collapse and closures. Already warned in January virus would hurt results. Closed 2000+ China stores. Investors extrapolating China-style disruption globally
secondary_factors: Exposure to urban foot traffic office districts and international markets. No new company release Mar 9-10
store_description: Starbucks was one of the earliest U.S. multinationals to quantify virus damage so the market had a template for what global spread could do. Once Italy locked down and COVID was labeled a pandemic investors likely assumed the China playbook would migrate to Europe and North America.

primary_cause: Aerospace exposure especially commercial aviation repriced sharply lower. Flights canceled borders tightened travel collapsed
secondary_factors: General cyclicals selloff and uncertainty around pending merger and integration backdrop. No fresh Raytheon/UTC merger headline
store_description: Even though Raytheon had defense exposure the future RTX combination also bundled in major commercial aerospace businesses highly sensitive to air-travel demand. As flights were canceled borders tightened and travel collapsed the market hit aerospace suppliers hard.

primary_cause: Smartphone-demand and supply-chain disruption fears. Mar 2 Qualcomm said China virus threatened phone-industry disruption. Kept 2020 5G handset estimate at 175M-225M
secondary_factors: Cyclical semiconductor selloff and global recession risk
store_description: Qualcomm had already explicitly warned that the outbreak threatened the phone industry so by March 11 investors were not waiting for another press release. The stock was being repriced for weaker handset shipments and supply-chain friction even though management had not yet cut its 5G handset outlook.

primary_cause: No fresh Philip Morris-specific catalyst. Broad market liquidation with concern about international distribution and disruption
secondary_factors: EM and currency exposure and general consumer-discretionary-like de-risking despite defensive nature of tobacco
store_description: PM's decline was larger than a normal defensive-stock move suggesting investors were selling globally exposed multinationals indiscriminately. Given its international footprint the market likely also worried about disrupted retail channels logistics and FX pressure as the pandemic spread.

primary_cause: STOCK-SPECIFIC context. Feb 20 P&G said coronavirus would hurt current-quarter revenue and profit from supply-chain disruption and weaker China demand. Prior virus warning repriced more aggressively as outbreak globalized
secondary_factors: Marketwide liquidation and concern supply-chain problems could outweigh demand for staples in near term
store_description: Unlike Walmart P&G already had a clear negative coronavirus warning on the tape before March 11. As COVID spread outside China investors likely assumed the hit would extend beyond the company's original geographic framing which helps explain why even a staples giant fell 7.4%.

primary_cause: Cyclical semiconductor derating on recession fears. Heavily tied to broad industrial and electronics demand. No fresh Texas Instruments-specific announcement
secondary_factors: Concern over weaker industrial and electronics demand and supply disruption. Market moving from supply-shock to demand-destruction narrative
store_description: Texas Instruments is heavily tied to broad industrial and electronics demand so it was a classic slowdown chip name during the COVID panic. With the market moving from a supply-shock narrative to a demand-destruction narrative TXN's 5.0% drop looks mostly like cyclical semiconductor repricing.

primary_cause: Expected slowdown in elective procedures using da Vinci systems. No March 9-10 Intuitive Surgical release
secondary_factors: Hospital resource diversion and capex caution. Later confirmed procedures fell to about 65% of earlier Q1 weekly levels in last half of March
store_description: Even before hospitals formally cut back investors could see the direction of travel: operating rooms and hospital staff were going to be redirected toward pandemic response. Later company filings confirmed that procedures in the U.S. fell to about 65% of earlier Q1 weekly levels.

primary_cause: No fresh Intuit-specific release. Mostly broad-market selloff. Relatively smaller 3.2% decline
secondary_factors: Emerging concern that small-business customers would weaken if economy shut down. Tax deadline extension and SMB pressure became clearer later
store_description: Intuit's relatively smaller 3.2% decline supports the idea that this was largely macro. The more direct company-specific COVID issue the tax deadline extension and SMB pressure became clearer later so on March 11 the move appears mostly to have been generalized risk-off selling.
